name: Progressivism
summary: Progressivism seeks deliberate social improvement through democratic reform, wider effective freedom and a fairer distribution of opportunity and economic resources. Its defining accounts support public action to counter concentrated power while differing over institutional design, ownership and the role of religion. Contemporary self-definitions also emphasise sustainability and cooperation.
scope: The political reform tradition described by Thompson (s28), CAP’s defining intellectual and human-rights studies (s17, s16), the Encyclopedia of Religion and Society (s9), and Compass’s account of progressive politics (s27). These sources discuss historical American progressivism and its later development, alongside a British definition combining democracy, equality and sustainability; the name is not reduced to a present-day US caucus. Croly’s The Promise of American Life and Dewey’s The Public and Its Problems count only as the specific seminal/canonical works that s17 identifies. An organisation’s account of progressive principles is used as a definition, not as authority for its wider platform. Historical exclusions and religious contributions are not removed by definition; a general observation that the movement varies does not itself answer a statement.

furtherReading.title: Progressivism — J. A. Thompson
furtherReading.note: A scholarly introduction to the tradition and its internal disagreements.

furtherReading.title: The Progressive Intellectual Tradition in America
furtherReading.note: A readable account of progressive values and their development.

furtherReading.title: On Being Progressive
furtherReading.note: A British organisation’s explicit discussion of the term and its limits.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: In Chapter X Croly says a peace-seeking democracy must be physically prepared to fight and advocates sufficient naval strength to sustain its foreign commitments.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: The creation of public regulatory agencies does not answer whether money should be left to the market and central banks abolished.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Workplace safety and efficiency proposals do not settle abolition of occupational specialisation.

abolish-income-tax.rationale: Thompson identifies income taxation as an explicit progressive means of paying for social provision and reducing unequal wealth.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Supporting wage protections does not settle the eventual abolition of money and wage labour.

abortion-legal.rationale: Shalin describes the defence of women’s reproductive rights against restrictive state laws and court decisions as part of contemporary progressive politics.

alienated-labor.rationale: The earlier answer treats a theory’s lack of centrality as a recorded middle position.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: The earlier answer assigns a presumed contemporary animal-welfare consensus without checked defining evidence.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: A caucus’s defence of democracy does not establish antifascism as a foundational national constitutional value.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The human-rights study identifies the UDHR as a statement of progressive values; Article 18 explicitly protects changing one’s religion or belief.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: The earlier answer assigns a presumed New Deal spending policy without a defining position on large stimulus deficits.

ban-cartels.rationale: Thompson distinguishes trust-busting progressives from the New Nationalist approach of regulating large combinations instead of breaking them up.

bound-labor.rationale: The earlier rationale acknowledges that its labour sources do not discuss legally binding cultivators to a lord.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: General equal treatment does not establish a stated position on consumer boycotts of minority-owned shops.

capital-controls.rationale: Financial regulation does not establish a position on controlling cross-border capital flows; the earlier rationale supplies no such evidence.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Shalin describes progressive reform as an effort to salvage capitalism through reconstruction instead of overthrowing it.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Advocacy of peace and regulated capitalism does not settle a theory about the causes of imperialism and war.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The intellectual history describes progressivism as retaining the gains of technology, industrialisation and capitalism while countering corporate power and unequal opportunity.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The earlier answer asserts a modern preference over an acknowledged historical censorship position without documenting a sustained ideological change.

central-bank-independence.rationale: The earlier rationale confuses a central bank’s objectives with its institutional independence from elected officials.

central-planning.rationale: Shalin defines the reformers’ project as reconstructing capitalism rather than adopting a command economy or massive nationalisation.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: The intellectual history describes laws and institutions as revisable when changed social conditions make inherited arrangements unable to serve freedom and democracy.

character-from-environment.rationale: Dewey’s Chapter V describes effective intelligence and social habits as developed through education, culture and institutions rather than fixed faculties present in isolation.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The intellectual history assigns government an organised responsibility for protecting people from insecurity; Croly’s Chapter XII rejects leaving wealth’s public duties to accidental private benevolence.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Croly’s Chapter VIII explicitly defends temporary colonial tutelage of Asian and African societies, while Compass’s definition criticises the colonial hierarchy of civilised societies ruling others as regressive.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Reforming class relations does not settle the proposition that class conflict drives history.

clerical-rule.rationale: The earlier answer derives rejection of religious scholars’ political authority from generic secularism and democracy.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Croly’s Chapter XII would set minimum wages and working hours through bargaining between employer organisations and unions while permitting additional individual rewards above the minimum.

collective-farming.rationale: The earlier answer reasons from the lack of a collective-farming plank and from unrelated public-land policies.

common-currency.rationale: The earlier answer asserts a monetary-union split without identifying opposed defining sources.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Thompson places government by the people at the centre of progressive political philosophy and explains reforms intended to make that authority effective.

corporate-influence.rationale: The earlier answer relies on one party’s campaign-finance plank; defining accounts of corporate political power concern a broader claim than lobbying and campaign funding specifically.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Support for unions and regulation does not settle compulsory state-recognised bodies setting wages and prices together.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Shalin describes contemporary progressivism as trying to correct the exclusion of racial minorities from earlier reforms and to address the legacy of segregation and discrimination.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: In Chapter VII Croly defends an independent judiciary’s duty to interpret the Constitution, while calling for a more amendable constitution rather than judicial subordination to passing majorities.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The earlier answer relies on a caucus’s LGBTQ programme rather than a checked defining position on criminal law.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The human-rights study describes progressive social provision of food, housing, education and health care as indispensable to the effective exercise of political freedom.

decide-locally.rationale: Croly’s national regulation and Dewey’s local public deliberation address different responsibilities; they do not establish opposed positions on a general rule that decisions belong at the most local possible level.

democracy-best.rationale: Thompson describes democracy as the core of progressive political philosophy, defended both as morally legitimate and as more reliable over time than rule by a few.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Croly’s Chapter VII says popular sovereignty can produce anti-democratic government; Dewey’s Chapter V likewise distinguishes democratic social life from its electoral machinery.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The earlier answer treats general reformism as a specific position on a postrevolutionary class dictatorship.

direct-action.rationale: Reform through elections does not exclude direct action, and the earlier answer does not establish a stated priority between them.

direct-votes.rationale: Thompson identifies initiative and referendum as progressive means of letting voters directly make or repeal laws.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: The earlier answer uses generic equality and a caucus position to answer a particular judgment about interracial families.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: The earlier answer assigns a caucus’s equity policies to a specific definition of discrimination by effect rather than intention.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Women’s suffrage does not settle all legally differentiated gender roles.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Social insurance and wages do not settle the ultimate principle by which all goods should be distributed.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Thompson identifies a more equitable distribution of wealth as a defining progressive aim and rejects treating existing fortunes as proof of personal virtue alone.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: A party’s popular-government platform does not settle the ultimate theological source of authority for the broad ideology.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: The earlier answer substitutes the caucus’s Green New Deal endorsement for a defining account of progressivism’s climate tenets.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The statement permits a leader’s child to succeed through an election; support for democratic accountability does not rule that out.

economic-freedom.rationale: Opposition to unregulated markets does not settle whether political freedom depends on economic freedom in the statement’s general sense.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: General nondiscrimination does not settle a specific rule about the ethnic ownership of the economy.

elective-rulers.rationale: The earlier answer treats elected leadership as necessarily excluding a constitutional monarch chosen by inheritance.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The human-rights study accepts limited, temporary derogations from some ordinary rights during genuine public emergencies while preserving nonderogable protections.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The human-rights study argues that international human-rights commitments need legitimate avenues of redress and actual enforcement powers against abusive states.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: The earlier answer assigns a caucus’s affirmative-action programme to the broad ideology.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Shalin describes progressive reformers’ commitment to retaining constitutional safeguards against one-party tyranny, while reconstructing economic and democratic institutions.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The human-rights study explicitly presents equal human dignity and rights as core progressive values, grounded in common humanity.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The earlier rationale asserts a split without identifying sources advocating and rejecting equality of outcomes as the goal.

equal-parenting.rationale: The earlier rationale asserts competing concerns instead of evidence on custody after divorce.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The earlier answer relies on general antidiscrimination and one party platform, without a defining position on national ethnic composition.

every-country-ready-for-democracy.rationale: Croly’s Chapter VIII explicitly claims that most Asian and African societies were not then capable of national democratic government and uses that claim to defend tutelage.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Valuing political participation does not settle the comparative importance of emigration and voting as checks on government.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: The earlier answer attributes the caucus’s energy programme to the broad ideology.

experts-over-public.rationale: Croly delegates technical details to specialists and Dewey requires popular control of policy; these concern different responsibilities and do not settle which group should have more overall say.

family-wage.rationale: The human-rights study treats the UDHR as a statement of progressive values; Article 23 in its appendix requires remuneration sufficient for a worker and family to live in dignity.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Thompson describes progressive income taxation as part of using public power to reduce wealth inequalities; Shalin expressly includes progressive income tax and inheritance surcharges among reform tenets.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: In Chapter IV Croly calls the Union’s military prevention of Southern secession justifiable coercion and rejects accepting peaceful disunion as the better course.

force-without-un.rationale: Multilateral cooperation does not settle whether force may ever be used without Security Council approval.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The earlier answer records an unknown foreign-land policy as a split.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: The earlier answer treats lack of a settled takeover policy as a documented split.

free-public-college.rationale: The earlier answer relies on a caucus’s tuition policy rather than a defining progressive rule for university funding.

free-trade.rationale: A protective tariff proposal does not settle whether every person benefits from free trade in the long run.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The earlier answer relies on a particular caucus programme rather than a defining account of private owners’ duties.

future-generations.rationale: The earlier answer turns historical conservation policy into a specific obligation to leave the Earth undamaged for future generations.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: General support for active government and gender equality does not settle creating dedicated equality agencies.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: The earlier answer relies on a caucus platform as the broad ideology’s doctrine of gender-identity law.

gm-crops.rationale: The earlier rationale explicitly says no settled position on genetically engineered crops was found.

gradual-change.rationale: Croly’s Chapter IX rejects suddenly uprooting essential national institutions and requires demonstrated need, discussion and public consent for substantial changes.

harm-principle.rationale: The earlier answer contrasts moral regulation with a related liberal tradition but does not establish progressivism’s own rule limiting state interference.

hereditarian-race.rationale: The earlier answer substitutes opposition to racism for a stated position on genetic explanations of group abilities.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Croly’s Chapter XI speculates that a regenerated state might investigate and favour enforced celibacy for hereditary criminals and people with incipient mental illness. This hypothetical investigation does not establish a settled prescription for reproductive restrictions on people with heritable defects.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: The earlier answer contrasts Americanisation with an unverified caucus stance rather than a documented position on compulsory language learning.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Labour protections and criticism of unearned wealth do not settle the exclusive claim that income should reward work rather than ownership.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: The earlier answer derives rejection of hereditary indigenous leadership from general equality and representation.

indirect-election.rationale: Thompson identifies direct popular election of senators, replacing election by state legislatures, as a central progressive reform.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Thompson says progressive writers welcomed industrial and technological possibilities and sought a fairer distribution of their benefits rather than abandoning industrial society.

informal-organisation.rationale: Reform through institutions does not state a preference about the internal formality of political organisations.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The human-rights study grounds progressive rights in the UDHR; Article 16 in its appendix explicitly rejects religious limitations on marriage.

internal-colonialism.rationale: The earlier answer asserts disagreement among unspecified adherents rather than evidence on the regional-exploitation theory.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: The human-rights study supports international accountability for crimes against humanity and describes the ICC as a mechanism to prosecute when national authorities cannot or will not act.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: The earlier answer attributes a caucus’s treatment of injustices to a general theory that oppressions cannot be addressed separately.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: General cooperation and restraint do not settle a state’s right to intervene in an allied country to preserve its political system.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The earlier answer derives a position on scriptural law from general democracy and human-rights commitments.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: The earlier rationale calls adherents divided but cites no opposed stated positions on legal sex work.

limit-growth.rationale: Compass’s defining account connects the costs of unchecked economic progress with the climate crisis and presents degrowth and redistribution as a potentially more progressive approach than growth-first policy.

limit-population.rationale: Eugenics and reproductive choice are different questions from actively limiting population growth.

local-production.rationale: General conservation does not settle a preference for local production; the earlier rationale expressly acknowledges that gap.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: General criminal-justice reform does not settle fixed statutory sentences for serious repeat offenders.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: The earlier answer uses reformist democracy to reject a claim about what kinds of market economy are possible under a communist party.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Thompson defines progressivism by its rejection of laissez-faire and its demand for public control of economic activity to reduce inequality.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: The earlier answer asserts a split without cited opposed positions on culture pacifying workers.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Dewey’s Chapter V explicitly rejects an economic determinism that overlooks how knowledge, communication and shared meanings change the consequences of industrial forces.

material-over-identity.rationale: The earlier answer assigns a presumed contemporary ranking of economic and identity issues without a defining statement of that priority.

means-match-ends.rationale: Compass explicitly says that means shape ends and uses this principle to judge which kinds of change deserve to be called progressive.

media-academia-power.rationale: The earlier rationale uses journalism’s watchdog role to answer a comparison of institutional political power.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Generic democratic accountability does not establish a specific position on military intervention as guardian of a political order.

military-superiority.rationale: Reducing military expenditure does not establish a position against maintaining military superiority.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Compass’s definition rejects a politics of hostility toward outsiders and treats respect for individuals and collaboration across groups as requirements of progressive politics.

minority-veto.rationale: Dewey’s Chapter VI defends majority decision after discussion, persuasion and a fair chance for minorities to become majorities; it does not give each dissenting group a veto.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Croly’s Chapter XII favours public ownership combined with private operation of municipal utilities, while distinguishing those responsibilities from direct public administration.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Democratic participation can coexist with a ceremonial hereditary head of state, so democracy alone does not settle this statement.

more-religion-public.rationale: The faith study calls for religious voices to renew progressive public discourse and moral action while retaining a role for the secular tradition.

municipal-businesses-mixed-economy.rationale: Thompson identifies municipal ownership of public utilities among progressive economic reforms within a wider system retaining private enterprise.

nation-first.rationale: The human-rights study rejects advancing national security without regard to legitimate means and favours international human-rights law and global political cooperation.

national-church-status.rationale: The earlier answer derives a rule about a privileged national church from presumed secularism and general equal treatment.

national-mission.rationale: The earlier answer asserts historical disagreement without documenting opposed defining positions on spreading a country’s form of government.

national-rebirth.rationale: Reformist methods do not settle whether a nation needs radical renewal after decadence.

national-self-determination.rationale: The earlier answer attributes Wilson’s Fourteen Points to progressivism without establishing them as its canonical programme.

native-born-offices.rationale: The earlier answer uses general equal citizenship to answer the specific eligibility of foreign-born citizens for high office.

natural-rulers.rationale: The earlier answer moves from political equality to a claim about natural differences in aptitude for rule.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The earlier answer turns disagreement over a label for regulated capitalism into a substantive middle position.

night-watchman-state.rationale: CAP’s defining account assigns government responsibility for business regulation, economic opportunity and social protection beyond defence, policing and property.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Thompson describes the progressive challenge to vested economic interests and to financial domination of government, aimed at replacing privileged influence with public control.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Support for public social provision does not establish a special moral duty belonging to the wealthy as a class.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The earlier answer uses an American presidency and unspecified foreign adherents to assert a split on ceremonial heads of state.

office-by-exam.rationale: Respect for expertise does not settle selection of public officials through competitive examinations.

one-party-rule.rationale: Shalin describes the progressive rejection of the Bolshevik one-party state and insistence on constitutional safeguards and democratic reform.

online-anonymity.rationale: The earlier answer asserts conflicting privacy and safety concerns without stated positions on online identity requirements.

open-borders.rationale: The earlier answer treats immigration reform as evidence about the eventual abolition of border restrictions.

open-government-data.rationale: Publicity about corporations and politics does not establish a rule for publishing government decision trails and citizen proposals.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: The earlier answer derives a specific military-service rule from a caucus’s general LGBTQ policy.

organic-representation.rationale: Reforms of primaries and elections do not settle representation through families and occupational bodies.

paid-care-work.rationale: The earlier answer treats paid leave and childcare policies as a position on paying for unpaid care work.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Popular sovereignty and stronger national government do not settle the institutional supremacy of parliament.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The intellectual history identifies greater democratic control over workplaces, homes, neighbourhoods and the environment as practical implications of progressive philosophy.

party-controls-media.rationale: In Chapter V Dewey requires free social inquiry and dissemination of its results and criticises censorship and control of opinion as obstacles to democratic public judgment.

party-own-road.rationale: The earlier answer treats a question’s communist setting as a documented middle position.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Support for particular women’s rights does not by itself state a structural theory of male advantage throughout society.

patriotic-education.rationale: The earlier rationale contrasts Americanisation with an unspecified modern attitude rather than evidence on patriotic school instruction.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: The intellectual history describes a national democratic community whose public power should protect workers and families from concentrated economic power.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: The earlier rationale acknowledges that its sources do not discuss personal oaths as the basis of political authority.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Accepting private enterprise does not answer the statement’s distinction between personal possessions and productive property.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The intellectual history describes corporate domination of public institutions and a corrupt political class as problems progressivism seeks to overcome.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Supporting regulation does not settle the statement’s specific contrast between agency rules and property-damage liability.

population-transfer.rationale: General minority rights do not state a rule on forced population transfer of a minority deemed hostile.

positive-liberty.rationale: The intellectual history explicitly distinguishes effective freedom to pursue chosen ends from the mere absence of legal restraint and makes material and social capacity essential to liberty.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: The earlier answer assigns a presumed modern preference about monuments without defining evidence.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Croly’s Chapter IX argues that reform must respect national traditions and cohesion, with fair notice, public discussion and consent before changing fundamental institutions.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The intellectual history defines the common good to include placing the concerns of the least well-off above narrow self-interest and privileged demands.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The earlier rationale expressly acknowledges that its sources do not discuss privately supplied justice and defence.

production-for-use.rationale: Regulation of profit-making businesses does not settle whether production should ultimately serve need rather than profit.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Criticism of monopolies does not itself deny that ownership profits exploit workers.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Croly’s Chapter X argues that America should help establish an international order enabling democracy abroad and condemns indifference to its spread in Europe.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Public regulation and expert discretion do not settle the required form of standing laws versus case-specific decrees.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Family policy and immigration policy do not establish opposed positions on incentives for childbirth.

property-franchise.rationale: The human-rights study presents the UDHR as foundational to progressive values; Articles 2 and 21 in its appendix require political rights without property distinctions and universal equal suffrage.

property-fundamental.rationale: The intellectual history describes progressivism’s rejection of fixed property rights that prevent government from addressing exploitation, suffering and inequality.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The intellectual history describes progressive property rules as subject to their social consequences and the good of the community rather than immutable individual entitlements.

public-access-to-information.rationale: In Chapter V Dewey makes publicity and the free dissemination of inquiry essential conditions for an informed democratic public.

public-money-creation.rationale: The defining account’s currency and credit reforms do not specify whether money should be created directly by government.

public-ownership.rationale: Thompson describes progressive proposals for public ownership of natural monopolies alongside rival proposals for regulated private ownership.

race-social-construct.rationale: The earlier answer uses a caucus’s racial-justice position as evidence for a specific claim about the scientific status of race.

racial-franchise.rationale: The human-rights study identifies equal civil rights regardless of race and universal political participation as progressive commitments; its UDHR appendix makes suffrage universal and equal.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The earlier answer derives a racial-organising split from reparations and general racial-justice commitments.

racial-pride.rationale: The earlier answer asserts different attitudes to racial pride without checked defining evidence.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The earlier answer relies on a caucus programme, while the defining scholarship documents deep historical disagreement over racial segregation rather than one continuous position.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: The earlier answer treats racial justice advocacy as a comparative judgment that racism is the main remaining obstacle.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Thompson identifies minimum-wage laws among the social-welfare measures progressive writers advocated, particularly for poorly paid women.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The faith study presents religious moral insight alongside secular inquiry as an enduring source of progressive public action rather than treating reason as the exclusive guide.

recall-officials.rationale: Thompson identifies recall as a progressive reform allowing voters to eject elected officials before their term expires.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Recall of elected officials does not settle a whole system of binding mandates and recallable delegates.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The earlier evidence combines immigrant opportunity, assimilation and a caucus programme without establishing an overall immigration level.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Thompson identifies extending government regulation over economic activity and curbing corporate power as defining progressive commitments.

rehabilitation.rationale: The earlier evidence concerns prison reform and incarceration rates, which do not by themselves establish rehabilitation’s priority over punishment.

reification.rationale: The earlier rationale substitutes a theory’s absence for a documented position on commodity relations.

religion-illusion.rationale: The presence of religious progressives alone does not establish a shared explanation of religion or a documented split on its eventual disappearance.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: The earlier rationale asserts a secular-religious split without defining evidence on religion’s causal role in women’s oppression.

religious-exemptions.rationale: General religious liberty and equality do not establish opposed positions on exemptions from otherwise applicable law.

religious-nation.rationale: The earlier answer assumes secular national identity despite defining scholarship’s account of religious national themes within progressivism.

restore-past-order.rationale: Compass defines being progressive as deliberately changing unjust existing arrangements rather than preserving an inherited order for its own sake.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The human-rights study’s foundational declaration expressly protects changing religion and manifesting belief in teaching and observance.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The earlier answer relies on general democratic and civil-liberty commitments rather than a specific position on temporarily restricting rights to accelerate growth.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: The earlier answer manufactures a split by putting general movement rights against indigenous rights without specific settlement evidence.

restrict-private-adult-pornography-acces.rationale: The earlier rationale asserts a cross-period split but supplies no checked defining positions on pornography law.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Supporting labour organisation does not settle particular legal requirements on strikes or picketing.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The intellectual history identifies judging ideas by their practical consequences, empirical evidence and experimentation as a central progressive value.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The earlier rationale expressly acknowledges that its sources never discuss returning to foraging.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The human-rights study argues for investment in development and essential services for the global poor as a responsibility grounded in universal freedom and security.

rich-first.rationale: Reducing inequality does not settle whether temporary differential enrichment can be a permissible route to development.

right-to-secede.rationale: Croly’s Chapter IV defends the Union’s coercive resistance to Southern secession and argues that national democratic responsibility cannot be displaced by local claims.

rule-by-example.rationale: Advocacy of laws and institutions does not determine the comparative importance of rulers’ moral example.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: The earlier rationale substitutes a connection to Gramsci and an asserted disagreement for the ideology’s own positions.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: The earlier answer assigns a caucus’s marriage-law policy to progressivism as a whole.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The intellectual history identifies the common good and the needs of the least well-off as priorities above narrow self-interest and privileged demands.

self-ownership.rationale: Bodily autonomy and taxation do not settle the philosophical doctrine of full self-ownership.

separate-church-state.rationale: The earlier answer combines French anticlericalism and a modern caucus position rather than a defining commitment to strict institutional separation.

separated-powers.rationale: Croly’s Chapter XI argues that dividing executive and legislative responsibility produces ineffective government and proposes concentrating responsibility in accountable elected leadership.

single-common-good.rationale: The earlier answer asserts a split without documenting incompatible positions on whether politics should pursue one rationally determined good.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: In Chapters IV and IX Croly identifies the conflict over slavery as the contradiction that made civil war necessary and describes its elimination as the war’s decisive national result.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Shalin describes progressivism’s method as reform and reconstruction of democratic institutions rather than revolutionary replacement of the state.

social-market-economy.rationale: The intellectual history describes a mixed economy in which public regulation and social protection preserve productive activity while checking concentrated private power.

socialized-markets.rationale: The earlier answer treats a missing ownership doctrine as a split; acceptance of regulated markets does not settle the condition that enterprises must be worker- or publicly owned.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: The earlier rationale treats the lack of a Soviet-economic doctrine as a split instead of an unknown position.

space-expansion.rationale: The earlier answer supplies a split from the lack of a space-settlement doctrine.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Religious and secular participation alone does not establish opposed doctrines about human nature and the proper purposes of politics.

state-as-business.rationale: In Chapter VII Croly argues that a state cannot serve merely as an impartial referee of private competitors: it must deliberately secure the community’s public purposes.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Treating government as an instrument of reform does not settle whether the state is essentially an instrument of class domination.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The earlier answer relies on a particular Green New Deal programme rather than a defining progressive commitment to strategic state investment.

state-harmful.rationale: CAP’s defining account makes active democratic government responsible for regulating business and securing social opportunity; government is an essential instrument of reform.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The earlier rationale rejects state atheism because it is not part of a reform programme, rather than citing a position on it.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: The earlier answer asserts an alliance-policy split without checked opposed defining positions.

strong-leader.rationale: Thompson describes progressive proposals to concentrate administrative authority in elected executives so they can carry out public programmes, paired with direct popular accountability.

student-debt-relief.rationale: The earlier answer attributes a caucus’s debt-cancellation policy to progressivism as a whole.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Extending direct democracy does not by itself establish a stated rule about suppression of political opposition.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The earlier answer assigns a caucus’s universal programme to a general choice between universal and targeted social spending.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Croly’s objections to high tariffs and his acceptance of trade bargaining as a policy instrument do not settle a general prescription for protecting domestic industry.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Croly’s Chapter XII advocates a graduated federal inheritance tax to reduce accumulated inequalities, with rates reaching twenty percent.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Thompson describes progressive income and inheritance taxation as a way to finance social provision and attack the unequal distribution of wealth.

taxation-theft.rationale: Thompson identifies income and inheritance taxes as legitimate progressive means of financing social reform and reducing unequal wealth.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The intellectual history describes the progressive response as recognising that new technology alone cannot solve persistent human problems and that institutions and social purposes must change.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Peaceful dispute settlement does not by itself rule out territorial or geopolitical expansion.

total-state.rationale: Democratic government and accountability do not establish the scope of state direction over every area of life.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: The earlier answer asserts an equivalence debate among adherents without checked defining sources on that comparison.

traditional-family.rationale: The earlier answer draws a family doctrine from a caucus’s marriage policies; the defining sources do not equate family protection with traditional family forms.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Democratic civic values do not settle whether uniformed national-service youth movements should be organised.

unions-good.rationale: In Chapter XII Croly calls unions the most effective machinery for improving workers’ economic and social position, while requiring them to serve the public interest.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The human-rights study identifies access to basic health care as an essential progressive social right that government must make effective.

universal-morality.rationale: The earlier answer uses Enlightenment origins to supply a specific doctrine of moral truth knowable by reason.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Civil disobedience and support for lawful institutions do not establish opposed positions on the natural-law claim that unjust laws are not law.

vanguard-party.rationale: The earlier answer uses reformism to assign a position on the working class’s need for a revolutionary vanguard.

voter-id.rationale: The earlier answer assigns a caucus position to the broad ideology, and voting access alone does not settle proof-of-citizenship and ID rules.

war-builds-character.rationale: The earlier rationale concerns peaceful dispute settlement rather than the possible effect of war on national character.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Thompson describes concentrated corporate wealth as a threat to independent citizenship, political democracy and government free from financial domination.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Equal rights at marital dissolution do not by themselves establish whether either spouse may initiate divorce without the other’s consent.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Compass defines progressive change as a collective responsibility requiring active participation and cooperation across civil society and political institutions.

women-distinct-values.rationale: The earlier answer asserts an internal disagreement over women’s values without checked opposed sources.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Legal and labour reforms do not settle whether women’s equality requires deeper economic change.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The foundational declaration protects property ownership without sex distinctions but does not address equality of inheritance rights, which the statement also requires.

women-suffrage.rationale: Thompson identifies women’s suffrage as a progressive reform required to make government by the people effective.

worker-ownership.rationale: The defining scholarship describes different forms of industrial democracy, but collective bargaining and co-partnership do not establish opposed positions on workers collectively owning their workplaces.

workers-councils.rationale: Using elected legislatures does not establish a defining position against workers’ councils as a basis of political power.

workers-own-party.rationale: Working through broad reform coalitions does not settle whether workers should have an independent party.

workplace-democracy.rationale: The intellectual history describes progressive democracy as extending citizens’ control over workplaces as well as government, homes and neighbourhoods.

notes: Later pass checked all statements, including candidates. Read the full CAP intellectual, human-rights and faith studies, Thompson’s scholarly pamphlet, Shalin’s article, Compass’s definition and the complete ThinkProgress article. Downloaded and searched Croly’s seminal book and Dewey’s named political text through the project Gutenberg tool and local corpus, across economy, government, society, world, liberty, culture, ecology, technology, means and globalism. The local reference library contains a Russell review of Dewey’s logic book, not an additional defining progressive political text. Public-office speech and vote corpora cover individual adherents, not the ideology’s own record; party-in-government measures are not treated as official-doctrine regimes. Original Wikipedia sources and the 1912 platform are retained for review history; no current answer rests on Wikipedia or a caucus programme. CAP article pages, Britannica, Oxford, Cambridge, Cairn, Paperity, Sage and Harvard Law Review pages returned HTTP 403; no refused page was retried. The accessible official CAP PDF copies were different copies of the works. GitHub searches found no full-report mirror. Routledge’s full entry is paywalled, so only its visible definition is used. The ThinkProgress article was read as a lead; its handbook excerpts do not license importing further unverified handbook claims. The validator rejected the ThinkProgress definition because its text says progressive rather than naming Progressivism twice; it is therefore not used for answers. Its related claims were checked against qualifying defining sources. Follow-up research concentrated on international affairs, nationalism, local versus central authority, religion, ecology and technology. Croly’s colonial-tutelage prescription is recorded against Compass’s opposed judgment as a split. His hypothetical discussion of an investigation into eugenic restrictions is documented in the nulling rationale rather than excluded as an embarrassing historical excess or converted into a settled policy. Modern sources and the specific canonical texts are distinguished in the rationales. The sources do not provide an ideology-wide position on newer technologies, specific emissions targets, nuclear power, indigenous autonomy or the many other remaining null questions.
